The platforms this package can segment

Source: R/platform.R
platform_defaults.Rd

distsamp was aerial by construction and is now aerial by default. A shipboard survey differs in three ways that matter, and this is where all three are written down.

Usage

platform_defaults(platform = c("aerial", "vessel", "ship"))

Arguments

platform

"aerial" (default), "vessel", or "ship" as a synonym for "vessel".

Value

A list with platform, kind (the PLATFORM_KIND level to keep), effort_args (for narwcr::flag_effort()), and distance_sources (for sighting_distances()).

What changes with the platform

Effort criteria

The handbook's altitude ceiling (8.A.1) is an aircraft criterion, and it cannot be widened into one that applies to a ship — a record with no ALT fails it at any height, because a missing value fails a criterion, so max_alt_m = Inf rescues nothing. The vessel defaults drop it instead (narwcr::flag_effort(max_alt_m = NULL)). Sea state and visibility apply to both, and are left alone.

How much this costs depends on the file, so measure it rather than assume it. Some programmes leave ALT empty on their vessel records and every one of them is excluded; others write the observer's eye height there, which passes an aircraft's ceiling comfortably and hides the problem until the records that are empty go missing. On one real extract of 1,037,180 vessel records, 338,562 had no ALT — 32% of the vessel effort, and 277 of 741 eligible sightings.

Right-angle distance sources

"angle" is \(h/\tan\theta\) from an aircraft altitude, and the "strip" code books are the Skymaster's and the AT-11's (8.A.31). Neither means anything on a vessel, so the vessel default is "exact" alone — a sighting position projected onto the track, which is geometry rather than platform. See sighting_distances().

Which records are kept

narwcr::classify_platform() labels each stretch from its median speed. The platform names the label to keep.

What does not change

LEGTYPE 5 and 6 mark shipboard records (8.A.21), but they mark a platform of opportunity — a ship that recorded what it saw while going somewhere. That is not a designed line-transect, and counting it as effort would put unsearched track into the denominator of a density estimate. So the vessel defaults keep legtype_on_effort = 2, a designated census line, exactly as the aerial ones do. A dedicated shipboard line-transect survey codes its lines LEGTYPE = 2 and needs nothing here; a POP file is not a distance sampling dataset and no argument to this package makes it one.

Segmentation itself is platform-free. Great-circle distance between consecutive fixes, splitting at breaks in effort, and cutting a track into lengths are all geometry, and a ship's track segments the same way a plane's does.

Naming

"vessel" is the documented spelling, because it is the PLATFORM_KIND level the filter actually compares against — nothing is translated on the way through. "ship" is accepted everywhere "vessel" is, and resolves to it.

See also

prepare_survey(), segment_survey(), sighting_distances(), narwcr::classify_platform()

Examples

platform_defaults("aerial")
#> $platform
#> [1] "aerial"
#> 
#> $kind
#> [1] "aerial"
#> 
#> $effort_args
#> list()
#> 
#> $distance_sources
#> [1] "angle" "exact" "strip"
#> 

# A vessel drops the altitude ceiling and loses the aircraft distance
# sources
platform_defaults("vessel")
#> $platform
#> [1] "vessel"
#> 
#> $kind
#> [1] "vessel"
#> 
#> $effort_args
#> $effort_args$max_alt_m
#> NULL
#> 
#> 
#> $distance_sources
#> [1] "exact"
#> 

# "ship" is the same thing
identical(platform_defaults("ship"), platform_defaults("vessel"))
#> [1] TRUE
